items.gloss: voiceless th: tongue between the teeth, air flows out; not an s
voiced th in this, they, other: tongue between the teeth, not a d
v: top teeth touch the lower lip; w: rounded lips, no teeth

items.term: w after a consonant: quick, twelve, sweet
items.gloss: kw, tw, sw use a rounded-lip w, never a v: not kvick, tvelve

items.term: final voiced consonants: bad / bat (German final devoicing)
items.gloss: keep final b, d, g voiced; the vowel before them is also longer
a final z keeps buzzing: eyes, raise, lose; do not say ice, race

items.term: initial s: sun, said, sorry (not z)
items.gloss: s before a vowel is voiceless: sun, not German zun; see, not zee

items.term: z vs. ts: zoo, zero, zone
items.gloss: English z is a buzzing z, never German ts: ZEER-oh, not TSEH-ro
short relaxed ih (ship, live, sit) vs. long tense ee (sheep, leave, seat)
æ needs a wide-open jaw (bad, man, had); e is mid (bed, men, head)
short central uh (cup, luck, hut) vs. open ah (cop, lock, hot)
tongue tip curls back and touches nothing; never rolled or in the throat

items.term: the /oʊ/ glide: home, go, phone (not hom)
items.gloss: the o in home, go, phone glides toward oo; not a pure German o
t after voiceless sounds (asked), d after voiced (played), id after t or d (wanted)
s after voiceless sounds (cats), z after voiced (dogs), iz after hissing sounds (buses)
most unstressed vowels shrink to a short uh: about, problem, today
short relaxed u (full, look, pull) vs. long oo (fool, Luke, pool)
l after a vowel or before a consonant: back of the tongue raised, darker sound
of ends in a voiced v (uv); off ends in f (awf)
j is voiced (jeep, job, German); ch is voiceless (cheap, chop)
one r-colored vowel in bird, work, learn, first; not German ö
work has the r-colored ur vowel; walk has aw and a silent l
singer has no g sound (SING-er); finger adds a g (FING-ger)
won't rhymes with don't (wohnt); want has an ah sound (wahnt)
spelling aloud: A is ay, E is ee, I is eye; not as in German
G is jee, J is jay; German speakers often swap them
breathe, with, smooth end in a voiced th, not a z
th is soft air between tongue and teeth, not a t: thank / tank
keep the th inside consonant clusters: munths, fifth; do not drop it
keep a final v voiced: save, prove, leave; not safe, proof, leaf
keep a final j voiced: badge, ridge, age; not batch, rich
ay glides toward ee (late, wait, sale); e is short (let, wet, sell)
luck, but, much have uh; look, put, book have a short oo
æ in bag, cat, ran vs. short uh in bug, cut, run
aw in bought, law, caught vs. the oh glide in boat, low, coat

items.term: short o in American English: hot, job, model
items.gloss: US hot, job, model use an open ah: haht, jahb, MAH-dul
the voiced zh sound: MEZH-er, YOO-zhoo-ul; not sh or j
sh is smooth (share, wash); ch starts with a t (chair, watch)
n uses the tongue tip; ng uses the back of the tongue

items.term: h at the start: heart / art
items.gloss: say the h: dropping it turns heart into art, hold into old

items.term: y at the start: year / ear
items.gloss: year starts with a y glide (yeer); ear does not
eer in here, near, beer vs. air in there, care, bear
all three endings sound the same weak er: DAHK-ter, DAH-ler
say every final consonant: askt, teksts; not ast or aks
v uses top teeth on the lower lip; b closes both lips
R is ar, Y is why, Z is zee in American English
these comparatives add a g sound: LONG-ger, YUNG-ger; singer has none
US uses the æ of 'cat' here, not the British ah: ask, not ahsk
ar in farm, card, heart vs. or in form, cord, horse
some -ed adjectives end in id: NAY-kid, WIK-id, RUG-id
th is not f: three / free, thought / fought

items.term: aspirated p, t, k: pin / bin
items.gloss: p, t, k at the start of a stressed syllable need a puff of air
s is a thin hiss (see, sort); sh has rounded lips (she, short)
many Americans say both the same (kaht); both pronunciations are fine
most Americans say all three words the same: MAIR-ee

items.term: s + consonant at the start: school, Spain
items.gloss: start directly with s: skool, not eskool; no vowel before it

items.term: st and sp at the start: street, speak
items.gloss: s stays s before t or p: street, not shtreet
kn at the start of a word: the k is silent (nyfe, nee)
the l is silent in half, calm, talk, walk, folk
the h is silent: AH-nist, OW-er; so 'an honest', 'an hour'
THOH: here -ough sounds like 'oh', as in although, dough
THROO: here -ough sounds like 'oo'; the same sound as threw
-ought sounds like 'awt': thawt, bawt; the gh is silent
here -ough sounds like 'uff': tuff, ruff, ih-NUFF
BIZ-nis: two syllables; the u sounds like i, the middle i is silent
MIN-it (sixty seconds) vs. my-NOOT (very small, very detailed)
leed (to guide, be first) vs. led (the heavy metal, lead pipes)
reed in the present; red in the past and past participle
liv (to live) vs. lyve (a live show, live data)
klohss with s (near, a close friend) vs. klohz with z (to shut)
SED and SEZ with a short e; not 'sayd' or 'sayz'
unstressed -age at the end is said ij: MES-ij, VIL-ij, IM-ij
-ture is said cher: NAY-cher, KUL-cher; not 'na-toor'
mb at the end of a word: the b is silent (klyme, thum)
b before t is silent: det, dowt; also in debtor, doubtful
t after s before -en or -le is silent: LIS-un, KAS-ul
EYE-lund: the s is silent; also in isle and aisle
AN-ser: the w is silent, as in sword and two
FOR-in: the g is silent, as in sign and reign
BIZ-ee: the u sounds like the i in 'is'
HURD, rhymes with 'word'; not like 'hear' plus d
NAH-lij: silent k; the vowel is ah, not the oh of know
teer (a drop from the eye) vs. tair (to rip)
yooss with s (a use, no use) vs. yooz with z (to use)
wind with a short i (moving air) vs. wynd (turn, wind a clock)

items.term: ch as k: character, stomach, technique
items.gloss: in many Greek-origin words ch sounds like k: KAIR-ik-ter, STUM-uk

items.term: ou as uh: country, double, cousin
items.gloss: ou often sounds like the u in 'cup': KUN-tree, DUB-ul

items.term: o as uh: among, oven, government
items.gloss: o sounds like the u in 'cup': uh-MUNG, UV-un, GUV-ern-ment
one weak syllable usually drops: EV-ree, DIF-runt, FAM-lee

items.term: g as j: logic, register, technology
items.gloss: g before e, i, y is often j: LAH-jik, REJ-is-ter; not a hard g

items.term: x as gz: exact, example, exist
items.gloss: x before a stressed vowel is gz: ig-ZAKT, ig-ZAM-pul
-sion is zhun after a vowel (decision), shun after s or l (mission)
-ate in nouns and adjectives is a weak 'it': KLY-mit, PRY-vit
-ine has three sounds: EN-jin, muh-SHEEN, dih-FYNE
wr at the start: the w is silent (ryte, rawng)

items.term: wh as h: who, whole, whose
items.gloss: these words start with an h sound; the w is silent

items.term: ea as e: head, bread, health
items.gloss: ea is a short e in head, bread, health, weather; not ee

items.term: o as oo: move, prove, whom
items.gloss: o sounds like oo here: moov, proov, hoom; not a German o

items.term: ea as ay: great, break, steak
items.gloss: ea sounds like ay here, not ee: grayt, brayk, stayk
eigh is ay in weight and eight, but eye in height
laugh has laf; daughter, caught, taught have aw; gh is silent
KAWF: here -ough sounds like 'off'; also trough
DEZ-ert (dry land) vs. dih-ZURT (sweet course): different stress and sound
chooz (present) vs. chohz (past); both end in a z sound
MUSS-ul: the c is silent, as in scissors and scene
sign has a silent g (syne); in signature the g is said
final -mn: the n is silent (AW-tum, KAH-lum, kun-DEM)
u after g or b is silent here: gess, gyde, bild
KWY-er, rhymes with 'fire'; not 'choyr'
RES-trahnt or RES-tuh-rahnt; the middle vowel is weak or dropped
the l is silent: kood, wood, shood; would sounds like wood
ik-SKYOOSS with s (a reason) vs. ik-SKYOOZ with z (to forgive)
DUZ, rhymes with 'buzz'; not 'dooz'; doesn't is DUZ-unt
EE-ther and NEE-ther are most common in the US; EYE-ther is also correct
bow rhymes with 'now' (bend forward) or with 'go' (ribbon, arrows)
woond (an injury) vs. wownd (past of wind, as in wound up)

items.term: s as sh: sure, sugar, insurance
items.gloss: the s sounds like sh: shoor, SHUG-er, in-SHUR-unss
here oo sounds like the u in 'cup': bluhd, fluhd
stress the syllable just before -ic or -ical: sy-un-TIF-ik, TEK-nih-kul
stress the syllable before -logy or -graphy: by-AH-luh-jee, jee-AH-gruh-fee

items.term: contrastive stress: I said blue, not green
items.gloss: stress the word you correct or contrast; it gets the strongest beat
the last new, important word in a phrase gets the main stress
normal wh-questions fall at the end: Where do you work?
yes/no questions usually rise at the end: Do you work here?
a falling tag expects agreement: It's cold, isn't it?
a rising tag asks a real question: You're coming, aren't you?
rise on each item, fall on the last: apples, pears, and plums
speak in short meaningful chunks with small pauses between them
unstressed was and were reduce to wuz and wer: it wuz fine

items.term: weak have / has in perfect tenses
items.gloss: unstressed auxiliary have reduces to uv or 've: the kids uv left

items.term: strong forms at the end: Where are you from?
items.gloss: small words keep their full vowel at the end: from, to, at
STRAT-uh-jee: stress on the first syllable, not German stra-te-GIE
THEER-ee stresses the first syllable, but thee-uh-RET-ih-kul: the stress moves
-ee usually takes the main stress: tray-NEE, gair-un-TEE, ref-uh-REE
-eer always takes the main stress: en-juh-NEER, vah-lun-TEER
stress the syllable just before these endings: fuh-NAN-shul, myoo-ZISH-un
-ique takes the stress and sounds like 'eek': tek-NEEK, yoo-NEEK
stress two syllables before -ate: KAHN-sun-trayt, DEM-un-strayt

items.term: two-syllable nouns vs. verbs: the basic rule
items.gloss: most two-syllable nouns stress the first syllable, most verbs the second

items.term: prefixes: stress on the root: unhappy, rewrite
items.gloss: prefixes like un-, re-, dis- are usually unstressed: un-HAP-ee, ree-RYTE
compound adjectives usually stress the second part: well-KNOWN, long-TERM
the article a is a short uh, not ay: uh book, un apple
unstressed are reduces to er: What er you doing?
unstressed at reduces to ut: look ut this, ut the office
unstressed from reduces to frum: a letter frum the bank
unstressed some (an amount) reduces to sum: I need sum water
already mentioned words lose stress; the stress moves to the new word
rise on the first choice, fall on the last: tea (rise) or coffee (fall)?
a statement with rising intonation works as a surprised question
repeat with a wh-word and a sharp rise to show surprise or ask again
fall-rise signals a reservation or an unsaid 'but': The talk was good…
rising Sorry? asks someone to repeat; falling Sorry. apologizes

items.term: flat intonation sounds bored or rude
items.gloss: English uses wide pitch movement; a flat voice sounds uninterested or unfriendly

items.term: street names: Main Street vs. Main Avenue
items.gloss: Street is never stressed (MAIN Street); Avenue, Road, Drive are (Main AVenue)
KAHN-sept: stress on the first syllable, unlike German Konzept
KAHN-tekst: stress on the first syllable; contextual is kun-TEKS-choo-ul
EK-spert: stress on the first syllable; German Experte stresses the second
fuh-LAH-suh-fee: stress on the second syllable, not on the end
FIZ-iks: stress on the first syllable, not German Physik
AT-mus-feer: stress on the first syllable, not German Atmosphäre
MEK-uh-niz-um: stress on the first syllable; the ch sounds like k
kuh-TAS-truh-fee: four syllables, stress on the second
yur-uh-PEE-un: stress on -pe-, not yoo-ROH-pee-un
PROH-gram: stress on the first syllable; programmer is PROH-gram-er
PREZ-ih-dent: stress on the first syllable; presidential is prez-ih-DEN-shul
MOH-ment: stress on the first syllable, unlike German Moment
US REE-sorss: stress usually on the first syllable
kuh-REER (stress on the end) vs. KAIR-ee-er (stress on the start)
unstressed than reduces to thun: better thun before
unstressed as reduces to uz: uz soon uz possible
the stress falls on -self or -selves: my-SELF, them-SELVZ
these suffixes keep the stress of the base word: CARE-ful, HAP-ee-ness
these words break the -ic rule and stress the first syllable
the first clause rises to show more is coming; the sentence then falls

items.term: pausing around extra information: My boss, who …
items.gloss: pause and lower the pitch around extra clauses set off by commas
rising at the end of statements; common among younger Americans, can sound unsure
say phone numbers in groups of 3-3-4; zero is often 'oh'
